name: Omar Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a marketing coordinator at a furniture brand, sofas, beds, mattresses, with twelve showrooms. I write the catalogue copy, plan the weekend sales, and send the posters and price cards out to each showroom. Thursdays are always busy because the weekend sale has to be live by Friday night.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's tiring?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like it when a sale works and the showroom managers ring to say they're busy. What's tiring is that I still make mistakes on the price cards, and my manager, Mrs Okafor, has to catch them. I use an AI tool now and then, mostly to tidy up product descriptions, once I saw the others were using it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what my father always said would happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it at the mosque after Friday prayers, half joking, that the machines aren't taking over after all. At work I'd just get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, if AI stays a gadget, I'll keep writing about sofas, and our weekend sales will still be won by a good photo of a comfy chair. My job's fine, we've got about eight months saved, and there are plenty of brands nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and work on my accuracy, so Mrs Okafor stops catching my mistakes. I'd use the tool a bit more for descriptions, since it saves an hour or two. Keep saving as we do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's 'we', when you say eight months saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Samira, my wife. She's a dental hygienist, so between us we're steady. We've been married a year and we're careful with money, like our parents were.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything here that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Furniture sales drop when people are nervous about money. If there's a bad year, they stop hiring and juniors get stretched. That's just business.

say: I'd joke at the **mosque** that machines aren't taking over after all.
I'd **get on with it** at work without fuss.
think: I think our sales will still depend on a **good photo** of a chair.
I'd feel secure with **eight months saved** and plenty of nearby brands.
do: Work on my **accuracy** so my manager stops catching price card errors.
Use the **AI tool** a bit more to save an hour on descriptions.
S0.quote: If AI stays a gadget, I'll keep writing about sofas, and our weekend sales will still be won by a good photo of a comfy chair.
fieldNote: He and his wife share **careful money habits** from their parents.
His only worry is the normal **furniture sales cycle**.
He picked up the tool **after others did**, true to his steady nature.

steps.text: Double-check every price card before Friday's sale goes live
Use the AI tool to tidy up more catalogue descriptions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like what's actually starting to happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses have to move with the times, and it's not the government's job to stop them. But I'd also say young people need apprenticeships into new work, not just being told to retrain online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, writing the catalogue used to take me three weeks, and if a tool does it in an afternoon, someone will ask what I do with the other twenty days. I'm the junior, so it's my days they'll count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly now that everyone's using them, maybe ask Mrs Okafor for a training day. I'd save another two hundred a month. And I'd help my father put his hardware shop online in the evenings, which gives me something solid if things go wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frightened. Like knowing a storm is forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why your father's shop, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's sold screws and paint for thirty years and he still does everything on paper. If I can get his orders online, that's useful to him and it's a skill I own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Darius, who does the showroom posters. His job is mostly resizing files, and I think the tools would eat it first.

say: I'd say businesses must **move with the times**.
I'd call for **apprenticeships** into new work, not just online retraining.
think: I think a three-week catalogue becomes **an afternoon**.
I'd expect my days as **the junior** to be counted first.
do: Ask my manager for an **AI training day** and save two hundred more.
Put my father's **hardware shop** online in the evenings.
feel: **Anxious** but not frightened, like a storm forecast.
S1.quote: Writing the catalogue used to take me three weeks, and if a tool does it in an afternoon, someone will ask what I do with the other twenty days.
fieldNote: He backs **free markets** but wants apprenticeships, not online courses.
His father's **shop** becomes his practical backup.
He worries about his colleague **Darius** before himself.

steps.text: Ask his manager for a day of training on AI catalogue tools
Save another two hundred a month
Set up online ordering for his father's hardware shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's very fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say communities and families will have to carry each other, and I'd say it at the mosque. I'd be wary of anyone promising the government will fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my desk job is gone soon after it arrives. My father has sold screws and paint behind the same counter for thirty years, and suddenly his little hardware shop looks like the safest job in the family. Samira's work is hands-on too, so she has a few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mrs Okafor I'm leaving, before she tells me, and join my father in the shop full-time, even for less money. We'd cut back hard, no holiday, no new car. And we'd lean on both families, we'd probably share Sunday meals and some bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel the weight of being the husband who lost his job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the shop make enough for two of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Barely. Maybe half my current pay. With Samira's wage and our savings, we'd manage for three years, then robots arrive and I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'the husband who lost his job'. Is that how Samira would see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. She'd say I'm being old-fashioned. But it's how I'd feel, and I can't help that.

say: I'd say **families and communities** must carry each other.
I'd be wary of promises that the **government** will fix it.
think: I think my **desk job** goes soon after AGI arrives.
I'd see my father's **hardware shop** as the family's safest job.
do: Leave before being pushed and join my father's **shop full-time**.
Cut the **holiday and car**, and share bills with both families.
feel: **Alarmed**, feeling the weight of being the husband who lost his job.
S2.quote: My father has sold screws and paint behind the same counter for thirty years, and suddenly his little hardware shop looks like the safest job in the family.
fieldNote: He sees the **hands-on** shop and his wife's job as buying three years.
His sense of being the **provider** drives the alarm more than money.
He'd choose to **leave first** rather than be let go.

steps.text: Hand in notice before redundancy comes
Work full-time in his father's hardware shop for about half pay
Skip the holiday and the new car this year
Share Sunday meals and some bills with both families

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to prepare, so people should get on with it rather than complain. I'd say young men especially should learn a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough time to put my savings into my father's shop and learn the trade properly before the catalogue writes itself. I'd stay at the furniture brand for a couple of years first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools fully at work to hold onto the job and the wage. I'd spend Saturdays in the shop learning the stock and the customers. Around 2029 I'd put about fifteen thousand into the shop, maybe a new counter and online stock, and join as a partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Samira think of that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She likes it, as long as we keep a cushion. We agreed we'd never put in more than half our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And when the robots come, around 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then a hardware shop needs someone who knows the customers by name. I hope. I'd be 35 and owning half a business, which is better than nothing.

say: I'd say there's **time to prepare**, so get on with it.
I'd urge young men to **learn a trade**.
think: I think five years lets me **learn the shop** properly.
I'd stay at the **furniture brand** a couple of years first.
do: Spend **Saturdays** in the shop learning stock and customers.
Put about **fifteen thousand** into the shop around 2029 and join as partner.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to put my savings into my father's shop and learn the trade properly before the catalogue writes itself.
fieldNote: His plan is **family ownership**, not a new employer.
He and his wife set a **limit**: never more than half their savings.
He hopes **knowing customers by name** outlasts robots.

steps.text: Use AI tools fully to keep the furniture job a while longer
Work Saturdays in his father's shop learning stock and customers
Invest about fifteen thousand to become a partner in the shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a proper amount of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for anyone not to prepare, and I'd say it kindly. Families should plan together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, with ten years, I'd do what my father did and build something the family owns, instead of waiting for a company to decide my worth. I'd lose the catalogue job at some point, but I'd go on my own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the furniture brand for four or five years and try to get promoted. Then I'd buy into the shop properly. Samira and I would plan to have our first child in the next couple of years, while things are calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's coming, but I can see how we'd manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why plan a child now, rather than wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because waiting for certainty means waiting forever. My parents had me with less money than we have now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father getting older before I'm ready to take over. The shop needs him until I really know the trade.

say: I'd say there's **no excuse** for anyone not to prepare with a decade.
I'd tell people that **families** should plan together, kindly.
think: I think I'd build something the **family owns**, like my father did.
I'd lose the **catalogue job** but go on my own terms.
do: Stay four or five years and aim for **promotion** first.
Buy into the **shop** and plan our **first child** soon.
feel: **Uneasy**, but I can see how we'd manage.
S4.quote: With ten years, I'd do what my father did and build something the family owns, instead of waiting for a company to decide my worth.
fieldNote: A decade lets him follow his **father's path** on his own terms.
He won't wait for certainty to have **children**.
His worry shifts to his father's **age**, not AI.

steps.text: Stay at the furniture brand and aim for promotion
Buy into his father's hardware shop in about five years
Plan a first child with his wife in the next two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time to learn the shop before I needed it. What would help is apprenticeships in real trades for people my age, and banks lending to small family businesses. Work isn't only about money for me; it's how a man shows his family he can be relied on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about small shops. Everyone talks about big companies and AI, but places like my father's could be where a lot of people end up.

headlineQuote: Work isn't only about money for me; it's how a man shows his family he can be relied on.
portrait: Omar is a 27-year-old **marketing coordinator** at a furniture brand with twelve showrooms.
He's married to Samira, a **dental hygienist**, and they have eight months saved.
He uses AI **now and then** and still makes price card mistakes his manager catches.
In faster pictures he turns to his father's **hardware shop**, which suddenly looks safest.
He blames no one, trusts **family and community**, and feels the weight of being a provider.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have no time to learn the **shop**.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** in real trades and bank lending to **family businesses**.
